Development of gluten tolerance in adult patients with celiac disease who have been diagnosed 20 years ago can be complex. While some studies suggest that it may be possible for individuals with CD to develop tolerance to gluten over time, others indicate that this process may not lead to permanent remission.

It is essential to note that genetic characteristics, particularly those involving HLA genotypes, may play a role in the development of gluten tolerance in these patients. Further research is needed to better understand the mechanisms underlying the development of gluten tolerance and to distinguish between CD patients who are at risk for developing tolerance versus those who require lifelong treatment.

It's also worth considering that some adult patients with CD may experience a long-term return to latency, where symptoms similar to those present before diagnosis may recur. In these cases, follow-up is crucial to monitor the development of gluten intolerance and adjust treatment as needed.

While more research is necessary to fully understand the relationship between gluten tolerance and celiac disease, it appears that some adult patients with CD may experience a gradual improvement in symptoms over time, while others remain symptomatic despite attempts at gluten-free living. Ultimately, individual responses to gluten exposure will vary, and ongoing monitoring and management are essential for those diagnosed with CD 20 years after diagnosis.
